headline: High: AutoGen’s code-execution defaults can leak or corrupt shared workspaces, while awesome-nlp adds no isolation or verification layer.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write files and execute shell commands in shared working directories, so prompt-injection via attacker-controlled file content is plausible. awesome-nlp is not runnable and exposes no ingestion surface, so the pairwise risk is mostly one-way from AutoGen’s outputs into files that could later be read as instructions. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF AutoGen is configured to read untrusted files from a shared workspace, injected instructions can be parsed as prompts.
IF a human copies AutoGen-generated text into another agent workflow, the bridge becomes manual and exploitable.
mitigations: Use a dedicated workspace per agent.
Store untrusted inputs in a separate read-only directory.
Add a short prompt-injection warning to file-ingest steps.
Review any file before passing it into AutoGen.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for files and outputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen touches application data and can write files while using broad network egress to configured model providers, so sensitive content may leave the local workspace. awesome-nlp is non-runnable and has no data-touching fields, so it does not add a second leakage path; the main concern is AutoGen exposing data it processes. The pairwise interaction is indirect and based on documented capabilities.
conditions: IF application data passed to AutoGen includes secrets or regulated content, model-provider egress can disclose it.
IF the workspace is shared with other processes, written artifacts may be readable outside the intended boundary.
mitigations: Restrict AutoGen to non-sensitive inputs.
Disable or narrow network egress where possible.
Use a per-run scratch directory and delete it after use.
Redact secrets before handing data to AutoGen.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP or content filtering on outbound prompts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen has shell, subprocess, filesystem read/write, and broad network egress, so it can contend for mutable local resources. awesome-nlp is not runnable, so it does not itself create a write conflict, but the pair still shares the same workspace if the operator places them there. Because the shared-state model is developer-defined, uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both are pointed at the same writable directory, AutoGen can overwrite artifacts used by other processes.
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking, concurrent runs can race on shared files.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Run only one writer per workspace.
Add a simple lock file before writes.
Keep awesome-nlp as a read-only reference artifact.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency locks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen can generate outputs from code-executing agents, but awesome-nlp is not runnable and has no downstream action-taking authority, so there is no strong evidence that its outputs are consumed as authoritative inputs. The pairwise cascade is therefore limited to manual reuse of AutoGen text, which is a weaker and smaller blast radius than the rubric’s medium case.
conditions: IF an operator copies AutoGen output into another workflow without review, errors can propagate manually.
IF a downstream system treats generated text as authoritative, the cascade becomes stronger.
mitigations: Require human review before reuse.
Mark generated text as untrusted.
Keep AutoGen outputs in a draft-only folder.
Add a checklist for factual verification.
requires-engineering: add citation/verification gates before action-taking.

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and application data, so compliance obligations depend on what the operator feeds it. awesome-nlp is a static open-source list with no runnable data path, so it does not materially add residency or retention risk. Because no specific regulated data class or jurisdiction mismatch is documented, this is a low, operator-controlled compliance concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is passed into AutoGen, retention and residency controls must match that data class.
IF model-provider logging is enabled, stored prompts may create a policy mismatch.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data to AutoGen.
Check provider retention settings.
Document what data classes are allowed.
Keep awesome-nlp as a non-processing reference.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing.
